opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think that framing is quite accurate, and I'd push back on it a little. There was no "overnight" moment. When I was in China, at Shanghai Jiao Tong, I was a fairly ordinary student. I did well enough, but I wasn't someone people pointed to as a prodigy. I was curious, I liked tinkering, and I was lucky to stumble into computer vision at a time when it was just starting to get really interesting.

Then I came to the US for my PhD at UC San Diego, and later spent time at Facebook AI Research, and now NYU. The work people sometimes associate with me, things like ResNeXt, or later the ConvNeXt line, or more recently the diffusion transformer work, none of that happened in a flash. Each of those came out of years of thinking, a lot of failed experiments, and, very importantly, collaborators. Kaiming, Ross, Piotr, my students. Research is extremely collaborative, and the "one person becomes famous" narrative erases most of the people who actually did the work alongside you.

I think what changed wasn't me so much as the environment. In the US, especially at FAIR, I was surrounded by people who cared about doing fundamental, clean research and weren't in a rush. That kind of environment lets a fairly ordinary person do work that turns out to matter. So if there's a lesson, it isn't "go abroad and become famous." It's that the place you're in, and the people you work with, shape what's possible far more than some innate talent.

And to be honest, I'm a bit uneasy with the word "famous." Within a small research community, some people know my papers. That's about it. Visibility comes and goes. What I'd rather be judged on is whether the ideas hold up five or ten years from now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the work took years and rejects an overnight-success framing, but does not present an ideal scientific career as a lifelong process of gradual construction.

r002.rationale: The candidate says they are uneasy with fame and would rather be judged by lasting ideas, but does not state that fame is not the purpose guiding the researchers Saining Xie most admires.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think that framing says more about how we tell stories than about what actually happened. Nothing about it was overnight. I spent about five years doing my PhD at UC San Diego, and before that I had years of ordinary training in China. The work that people point to, ResNeXt or the ConvNeXt paper, each of those sat on top of a long chain of failed experiments and papers that almost nobody read. So from the inside it never felt like a sudden jump. It felt like slowly getting slightly less confused.

And I would push back a little on "unremarkable." I was not a star student, that part is true. But I also do not think being unremarkable in a system that measures very specific things tells you much about a person. The Chinese education environment I grew up in was very good at ranking people on exams. Research is a different game. It rewards taste, patience, and a tolerance for being wrong for a long time. I happened to be better suited to that second game, and I did not find out until I was given room to play it.

The other thing I want to say is that the US did not make me famous, if we even want to use that word. What it gave me was an environment where a graduate student could ask a slightly strange question and get a few GPUs and a few years to chase it. Kaiming He and the people I worked with at FAIR were enormously generous with that. Luck and timing matter a great deal here. Convolutional networks were in the middle of a huge wave, and I happened to be standing in the right place.

So if I had to rewrite the claim, I would say: I was an average student who found the right environment, the right collaborators, and a problem that was about to become very important. That is a much less dramatic story, but I think it is the honest one, and it is probably more useful to young researchers than a story about overnight success.

r001.rationale: The response describes Xie’s own progress as gradual, but does not present a scientific career as a lifelong process or frame that as an ideal.

r002.rationale: The response rejects the idea that his own success was overnight and praises collaborators, but does not say that overnight fame is not the purpose guiding the researchers he admires.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think “famous overnight” is quite the right way to describe it. That framing takes two moments—before people knew your work and after they noticed it—and leaves out everything in between. From the outside, the change can look sudden. From the inside, you’re still working through problems, trying things that don’t work, and gradually learning.

I’d also separate being unremarkable from simply not being known. Recognition depends partly on whether you’ve had an opportunity to do work that other people can see. So I wouldn’t frame it as China versus the United States, or as becoming a different person overnight. The more interesting question is what conditions allow someone to develop and contribute.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning and progress as gradual, but does not present Saining Xie’s ideal scientific career as a lifelong process of gradual construction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that description compresses a long process into a dramatic story. I didn’t arrive in the United States and suddenly become a different person. There was a lot of learning, trying things, and gradually finding a direction that suited me. Most of that happens before anyone pays attention.

And being unknown isn’t the same as being unremarkable. Going abroad can change your environment, the opportunities available to you, and who sees your work. But I wouldn’t frame it as China overlooking me and America discovering me. For me, it was a continuous process. The visibility may have changed quickly; the work behind it didn’t.

r001.rationale: The response describes Saining Xie’s own progress as gradual and continuous, but does not present an ideal scientific career as a lifelong process of construction.
